title: Sensor Ring
statement: A sensor keeps only its most recent readings in a ring buffer with room for capacity readings. write(v) stores a reading; if the buffer is already full, the oldest reading is overwritten. read() removes and returns the oldest reading, or null if the buffer is empty. newest() returns the most recently written reading still in the buffer without removing it, or null if the buffer is empty. size() returns how many readings are stored. Given operations such as ["write", 5], ["read"], ["newest"] and ["size"], apply them in order to an empty buffer and return the results of every read, newest and size call, in order. write calls produce no result.
constraints: Each operation is exactly ["write", v], ["read"], ["newest"] or ["size"]

examples.explanation: Writing 4 into a full buffer overwrites the oldest reading (1). read() then returns 2, newest() is 4, and 2 readings (3 and 4) remain.
An empty buffer returns null for read, 0 for size and null for newest.

hints.content: A buffer with a fixed capacity never needs more than capacity slots.
An array with push and shift behaves correctly, but shift moves every remaining element.
Instead of moving elements, remember the index of the oldest reading and how many readings are stored.
The slot for the next write is (head + count) % capacity. When the buffer is full, write into the head slot and advance head, so the oldest reading is overwritten.
read returns slots[head], advances head and lowers count. newest is at (head + count - 1) % capacity. size is count.

testCases.explanation: A capacity-1 ring keeps only the latest write.
The head wraps past the end of the storage.
Negative values and zero are ordinary readings.
A large mixed workload on the largest buffer.

solutions.title: Array with push and shift
solutions.intuition: Keep the readings in an array in arrival order and drop from the front when it grows past capacity.
solutions.approach: write pushes and shifts once if the array is longer than capacity; read shifts; newest looks at the last element; size is the array length.
solutions.pseudocode:
kept = []
write v: kept.push(v); if kept.length > capacity: kept.shift()
read: kept.shift() or null
newest: last of kept or null
size: kept.length
solutions.timeComplexity: O(capacity) per write on a full buffer and per read, because shift moves the remaining elements
commonMistakes: Shifting before pushing, which drops a reading too early when the buffer is exactly full.
Returning undefined instead of null on an empty buffer.
solutions.interviewExplanation: This models the behaviour with an ordinary array. It is correct and short, but every shift moves the remaining elements, so a full buffer pays O(capacity) per write. A ring buffer removes that cost.

steps.title: Fill the array
steps.content: Writes 1, 2, 3 give [1, 2, 3]; writing 4 gives [1, 2, 3, 4], which is shifted to [2, 3, 4].

steps.title: Answer the queries
steps.content: read shifts 2, newest is 4, size is 2.

solutions.title: Fixed array with a head index
solutions.intuition: Never move readings. Keep the position of the oldest reading and the count, and wrap indexes with a remainder.
solutions.approach: Allocate capacity slots. Track head (oldest) and count. A write goes to (head + count) % capacity when there is room; when full it replaces slots[head] and head advances. read, newest and size are index arithmetic.
solutions.pseudocode:
slots = array(capacity); head = 0; count = 0
write v: if count == capacity: slots[head] = v; head = (head + 1) % capacity
         else: slots[(head + count) % capacity] = v; count += 1
read: if count == 0: null else v = slots[head]; head = (head + 1) % capacity; count -= 1
newest: slots[(head + count - 1) % capacity]
commonMistakes: Advancing head on every write instead of only when the buffer is full.
Computing newest as slots[head + count] without subtracting one, or without the wrap-around remainder.
solutions.interviewExplanation: A ring buffer stores readings in a fixed array and treats it as circular: head marks the oldest reading and count says how many are live, so the newest sits at head + count - 1 modulo the capacity. Every operation is constant time and the memory never grows beyond capacity. The invariant is that live readings occupy count consecutive slots starting at head, wrapping around.

steps.title: Fill to capacity
steps.content: With capacity 3, writes 1, 2, 3 occupy slots 0, 1, 2 with head 0 and count 3.

steps.title: Overwrite
steps.content: Writing 4 replaces slot 0 and head becomes 1, so the live readings are 2, 3, 4 in order.

steps.title: Query
steps.content: read returns slots[1] = 2 and head becomes 2; newest is slots[(2 + 2 - 1) % 3] = slots[0] = 4; size is 2.
